q: The Collegium for appointment of Supreme Court judges comprises:
explanation: Third Judges Case (1998): SC collegium = CJI + 4 senior-most puisne judges. HC collegium = CJI + 2 senior-most + the concerned HC CJ. NJAC (99th Amdt, 2014) tried replacing it — struck down 2015 (4:1).

q: The theory of basic structure of the Constitution was propounded in:
options: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
Golak Nath v. State of Punjab
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
explanation: Kesavananda (1973, 7:6): Parliament may amend any part but cannot destroy the basic structure. Golak Nath (1967) held FRs unamendable (later reversed by the 24th Amdt); Minerva Mills (1980) applied basic structure to strike 368(4)(5).

q: Under Article 143, the President can seek the Supreme Court's advisory opinion. The opinion is:
options: Equivalent to a judgment under Art 141
Not binding on the President — and the SC may refuse references except pre-constitutional treaty matters
explanation: Art 143(1): advisory, not binding on the President; SC may decline. Exception: 143(2) disputes involving pre-constitutional treaties etc. — SC is bound to report (duty, still not binding on the President).

q: Which writ is issued to quash an order already passed by a lower court or tribunal?
explanation: Certiorari = curative (quashes a passed order); Prohibition = preventive (stops proceedings before completion). Mandamus commands a public duty; habeas produces a detainee.

q: Statement I: Article 226 is wider than Article 32. Statement II: Art 226 covers fundamental rights and any other legal rights. Choose:
options: Both true; II does NOT explain I
explanation: 226 is wider (FRs + legal rights, any cause) — that IS why it is wider; 32 is a guaranteed right (Ambedkar's 'heart and soul'), FRs only. Note: 32 is part of the basic structure; suspension only under 359.

q: A Supreme Court judge can be removed on grounds of:
options: Violation of the code of conduct
explanation: Art 124(4): removal = President on an address by both Houses (special majority: majority of total + 2/3 present & voting) for 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity'. Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968: 100-MP motion → Speaker/Chairman → 3-member committee.

q: The age of retirement of a High Court judge is:
explanation: HC judges retire at 62; SC at 65. The 3-year gap is a deliberate juniority signal (HC→SC elevation gains 3 years).

q: Public Interest Litigation in India was pioneered by Justices:
options: V. Krishna Iyer and H.M. Kania
P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer
explanation: Justices Bhagwati & Krishna Iyer relaxed locus standi (S.P. Gupta 1981; Mumbai Kamgar Sabha 1976 line) — PIL for the poor. Hussainara Khatoon (1979) — from Bihar's prisons — proved the model.

q: The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India under:
explanation: Art 141: SC's declared law binds all Indian courts (not the SC itself — larger benches may revisit). Art 142 = complete justice; 143 = advisory; 140 = ancillary powers.

q: The Patna High Court was established in:
explanation: Patna HC established 1916 (Letters Patent, after the 1912 Bihar-Orissa separation created the province; earlier the Calcutta HC's Patna Bench). 2026 = its 110th anniversary year.

q: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979) established:
options: Right to vote in local elections
Right to strike for government employees
Right to speedy trial as a fundamental right
Right to property as a fundamental right
explanation: Bihar prisoners' PIL: speedy trial = FR (Art 21); free legal aid = right; undertrials' release orders followed. A PIL-landmark with a Bihar anchor — BPSC's dream combo.

q: The Supreme Court's original jurisdiction under Article 131 covers:
options: Disputes between the Centre and states, or among states
explanation: Art 131: Centre↔state, state↔state disputes (federal jurisdiction) — exclusive to the SC, excluding matters with interim pre-constitution remedies or covered elsewhere.

q: Under Article 136, the Supreme Court may grant special leave to appeal from any judgment/order of any court/tribunal. This is:
options: A matter of right for the appellant
Discretionary — a plenary power without parallel in other federations
explanation: Art 136 SLP = discretionary, exceptional, any court/tribunal (except military tribunals) — wider than any apex court's cert power elsewhere.

q: The NJAC Act and the 99th Constitutional Amendment were struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015 because:
options: The commission's composition threatened judicial independence — part of the basic structure
Parliament lacked the power to amend appointment rules
explanation: NJAC (CJI + 2 senior judges + Law Minister + 2 eminent persons) was struck down 4:1 (2015): executive voice in appointments compromised judicial independence — part of the basic structure. The Court thereby preserved the collegium.

q: District judges in a state are appointed by:
options: The Governor in consultation with the High Court
explanation: Art 233: Governor in consultation with the HC appoints district judges (Shetty 1992 barred executive discretion). Bihar's recent district-judge recruitment litigation (2024-25) tests this.

q: Which Article empowers High Courts to issue writs?
explanation: Art 226: HC writs for FRs + legal rights (territorial + cause-based jurisdiction post-15th Amdt). 227 = superintendence (administrative); 32 = SC's FR writs.

q: The Supreme Court is a court of record under:
explanation: Art 129: SC = court of record (powers to punish contempt — 129(2)); HCs under Art 215. Contempt of Courts Act 1971 (civil + criminal categories).

q: Statement I: Habeas corpus literally means 'to have the body of'. Statement II: It can be sought against both public and private detention. Choose:
options: Both true; II does NOT explain I
explanation: Habeas = 'you may have the body' (produce the detainee); available against private detention too (the only writ against private parties) — but that availability doesn't explain the literal meaning — II is independent.

q: The first woman judge of the Supreme Court was:
explanation: Justice M. Fathima Beevi (1989) — first woman SC judge. Ruma Pal (2000) much later; Indu Malhotra (2018) was the first woman lawyer directly elevated from the Bar.

q: 'Procedure established by law' in Article 21 was transformed into substantive due process in:
options: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
explanation: Maneka (1978): procedure must be fair, just, reasonable — importing due-process substance into Art 21. ADM Jabalpur (1976) is the discredited detention case (overruled 2017); Gopalan was the narrow original reading.

q: The number of Supreme Court judges (including the CJI) currently sanctioned is:
explanation: SC (Number of Judges) Amendment 2019: CJI + 33 = 34 (from 31). Original 1950: CJI + 7; growth over the decades to 34.

q: Art 227 superintendence of High Courts extends over:
options: All courts and tribunals in the state except military courts
explanation: Art 227: HC superintendence over all courts/tribunals except military (session courts, family, labour, etc.); L. Chandra Kumar (1997) restored tribunal judicial review through HCs/SC.

q: In the Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968 process, the 3-member inquiry committee comprises:
options: An SC judge + an HC Chief Justice + a distinguished jurist
explanation: Committee: SC judge + HC CJ + distinguished jurist (1968 Act). Motion: 100 MPs (LS) / 50 (RS) notice → presiding officer's admission → committee report → both Houses' special-majority address → President's order.

q: The electoral bonds scheme was struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2024 primarily violating:
options: Voters' right to know under Article 19(1)(a) — with Art 14 proportionality failure
explanation: Feb 2024: electoral bonds scheme unconstitutional — voters' right to know (Art 19(1)(a)); the scheme's anonymity + unlimited corporate funding also failed Art 14 proportionality. SBI was directed to disclose.

q: Match the PIL case with its domain: Hussainara (1), Olga Tellis (2), Vishaka (3), MC Mehta (4). Domains: (a) environment, (b) workplace harassment, (c) speedy trial, (d) pavement dwellers' rights:
explanation: Hussainara = speedy trial (Bihar, 1979); Olga Tellis = pavement dwellers (1985); Vishaka = workplace harassment guidelines (1997); MC Mehta = environment (Ganga/oleum gas series, 1986-).
